title: Balanced server design objectives
where_in_paper: Introduction / design objectives or guiding principles
decision: POWER4 was targeted at high single-thread performance, high system throughput, and server-grade reliability rather than optimizing only one of those axes.
alternatives_or_rejected: I do not recall a specific named rejected architecture. The implicit contrast is a one-dimensional design that chases only frequency, only multiprocessing scaling, or only reliability, which the paper suggests would be insufficient for high-end servers.
rationale: Enterprise server workloads need fast response time for individual threads, high aggregate throughput, and high availability; a server microprocessor had to address all three.
outcome: The paper presents POWER4 as an out-of-order server processor family with microarchitecture, cache, SMP, and RAS features aimed at those combined objectives.
weakest_point: Whether the paper explicitly states the objectives as a balanced three-way set, or whether I am compressing a broader introduction into that shape.
provenance_note: The objective itself is likely from the paper; the phrasing is my reconstruction, not a quotation.

title: On-chip L2 with off-chip L3 capacity
decision: POWER4 used an on-chip L2 cache together with a large off-chip L3 cache, rather than relying on on-chip cache alone for server capacity.
alternatives_or_rejected: The implicit alternatives were a much larger on-chip cache, which would cost area and possibly frequency, or too little off-chip cache, which would hurt server workload capacity. I am not certain the paper enumerates these alternatives explicitly.
rationale: Server workloads need large cache capacity, but on-chip cache is limited by die area, power, and latency; splitting the hierarchy balances low latency with large effective capacity.
outcome: The described cache hierarchy gave POWER4 systems low-latency on-chip caching plus large system-level cache for server workloads.
weakest_point: Exact cache sizes, sharing structure, and whether the L3 choice is presented as an explicit trade-off rather than a system fact.
provenance_note: The hierarchy is from the paper/chip; the explicit trade-off wording may be partly inferred.

title: RAS treated as a first-class design requirement
where_in_paper: RAS / reliability, availability, and serviceability section
decision: POWER4 incorporated extensive error detection, correction, retry/recovery, and serviceability features as part of the system microarchitecture rather than treating them as optional add-ons.
alternatives_or_rejected: A minimal-checking design would reduce complexity, but it would be incompatible with enterprise-server availability goals. I do not recall the paper naming specific rejected RAS architectures.
rationale: POWER4 was aimed at high-end servers where availability, fault containment, and serviceability are critical, so RAS had to be designed into the system from the start.
outcome: The paper reports a broad set of RAS mechanisms intended to allow detection, recovery, and service without unnecessary system downtime.
weakest_point: Which specific RAS mechanisms are described in this paper versus other POWER4 documentation or the companion physical-design paper.
provenance_note: The RAS emphasis is likely from the paper; the mechanism list may be influenced by general POWER4 knowledge.

title: High-frequency target with power/thermal control
where_in_paper: Clocking / power management or design-principles discussion
decision: POWER4 pursued high clock frequency for single-thread performance while including mechanisms to manage or throttle frequency under power and thermal limits.
alternatives_or_rejected: A fixed conservative frequency would simplify thermal and power design but would sacrifice performance. I am not certain the paper explicitly frames that as the rejected alternative.
rationale: High frequency improves performance, but server systems must remain within power and thermal envelopes across workloads; dynamic control lets the chip run fast when possible and back off when necessary.
outcome: The paper describes POWER4 as able to operate at high frequency while controlling power/thermal conditions, rather than simply choosing a lower fixed frequency.
weakest_point: Whether clock throttling/power management is discussed in this system-microarchitecture paper or mainly in the companion circuit/physical-design paper.
provenance_note: The high-frequency objective is likely from this paper; throttling details may be mixed with general POWER4 knowledge.
